title: Investigation of the effectiveness of applying ChatGPT in Dialogic Teaching Using Electroencephalography
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can effectively take on a dialogic teaching role similar to a human instructor in higher education. The core question is whether a large language model can support student learning through back-and-forth instructional dialogue, and how this compares with dialogue led by a human teacher. The study also uses electroencephalography (EEG) to explore differences in students’ cognitive activity while interacting with ChatGPT versus a teacher.

The intervention involved dialogic teaching on a unit about histogram equalization in a digital image processing course. Thirty-four undergraduate science and engineering students who had not previously taken the course were randomly assigned to one of two groups: an experimental group that learned through dialogue with ChatGPT, and a control group that learned through dialogue with a trained graduate student acting as the teacher. Students completed pretesting, then engaged in a short instructional dialogue session lasting about three to ten minutes, followed by a brief break, posttests assessing knowledge retention and transfer, and subjective evaluation forms. EEG data were recorded throughout the dialogue process.

The study was conducted at a large research university in Northwest China with undergraduate students only; it was not a K-12 study and did not address foundational reading outcomes. Thus, for the retrieval topic focused on causal evidence for generative AI and foundational reading in K-12 classrooms or school-supported settings, this paper does not provide direct relevant evidence. It is instead adjacent evidence from higher education in an information-related course.

The main findings were that the ChatGPT and human-teacher groups performed similarly on the retention test, but the human-teacher group scored higher on the transfer test, although the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Students also rated the human teacher more favorably for problem solving and preference. EEG results suggested higher theta-band activity, and some higher gamma-band activity, in the ChatGPT group, which the authors interpret as indicating increased cognitive engagement and attention during dialogue. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may help with basic knowledge acquisition but does not fully match human teachers for deeper knowledge application or creativity, and they recommend combining ChatGPT with traditional teaching rather than replacing teachers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small randomized experiment, which strengthens internal validity, but it is not K-12, not focused on reading or foundational literacy, and reports limited outcome measurement and no effect sizes/confidence intervals. It is therefore only adjacent evidence for the user’s target question rather than strong directly relevant classroom evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The main academic results show no significant advantage for ChatGPT and a negative directional trend on transfer relative to human teaching. For the target evidence question on K-12 foundational reading, this paper provides no direct causal support and only weak adjacent evidence outside mainstream literacy contexts.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a dialogic teaching agent for undergraduate students learning a digital image processing unit on histogram equalization, answering students’ content questions during a short instructional dialogue.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized comparison with 34 undergraduate students (n=17 ChatGPT, n=17 human teacher), ChatGPT-supported dialogic teaching produced retention scores similar to the human-teacher condition but lower transfer performance. Retention posttest means were 32.29 (SD=5.42) for ChatGPT versus 32.53 (SD=4.87) for human teacher, t=0.133, p=0.895; transfer means were 28.59 (SD=8.54) versus 33.06 (SD=7.60), t=1.612, p=0.117, indicating no statistically significant difference but a negative trend for ChatGPT on knowledge application.
finding.measure: Knowledge retention test and knowledge transfer test in undergraduate digital image processing (histogram equalization)
finding.std_deviation: Retention: ChatGPT SD=5.42, Human teacher SD=4.87; Transfer: ChatGPT SD=8.54, Human teacher SD=7.60

finding.finding_summary: Students rated the human-teacher condition more favorably than the ChatGPT condition on perceived problem-solving proficiency and liking for the dialogue. In the preference ratings, 11 of 17 human-teacher students gave the top score of 5 versus 2 of 17 in the ChatGPT group; for problem-solving proficiency, 5 of 17 human-teacher students gave a 5 versus 1 of 17 in the ChatGPT group.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of perceived problem-solving proficiency and liking/enjoyment of the dialogue

finding.finding_summary: The study specifically interprets knowledge transfer as deeper understanding, application, and innovation, and ChatGPT underperformed the human-teacher condition on this dimension. ChatGPT group mean transfer score was 28.59 (SD=8.54) versus 33.06 (SD=7.60) in the human-teacher group, t=1.612, p=0.117; although not statistically significant, the observed pattern suggests weaker support for application/creative transfer.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer test requiring application of learned content to a new problem context
